steps.body: When data spreads over many values, individual dots get crowded. A **histogram** groups values into equal-width **bins** and draws one bar per bin, its height showing how many values landed there. Ten quiz scores binned by fives — 0-4, 5-9, 10-14, 15-19 — give bars of height 1, 2, 4, 3. The bars **touch** because the bins share edges.
A histogram groups values into intervals, so its bars touch — there's no gap between one bin and the next. Set each bar to the count for its range.

widget.prompt: Build the histogram of minutes read: 0–9 has 3, 10–19 has 6, 20–29 has 4, 30–39 has 2.
widget.successFeedback: That's the histogram — bars touch because the bins are continuous ranges, and the tallest shows where most readers land.
widget.partialFeedback: Some bins are the wrong height. Each bar counts how many readers fall inside that interval.

cml.actionGoal: Build bars from a shared scale and coordinate category counts with visual height.

predict.prompt: A histogram's bars touch, with no gaps between them. That is because…

options.label: The bins sit next to each other on a number line, with nothing in between
The bars are always the same height
It simply looks tidier that way

predict.reveal: The bins run along a number line, and there is no space between "10–19" and "20–29" — a reading of 19.5 has to land somewhere. Bar charts separate their bars because their categories genuinely are separate things; a histogram cannot, because its categories are stretches of one continuous scale.

widget.prompt: In the scores histogram, how many students landed in the 10-14 bin?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 reads the bin's LABEL (its starting value). The COUNT is the bar's height: 4.
14 is the bin's upper edge, not the count. Bar height gives the count: 4 students.

steps.body: Bars sum to the data size.
explanationVariants: 1+2+4+3 = 10 — every data value lands in exactly one bin, so bar heights total the data size.
The histogram accounts for every value once: heights sum to 10.

widget.prompt: The four bars have heights 1, 2, 4, 3. How many quiz scores were collected in total?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 counts the BARS (bins), not the scores inside them. Add the heights: 1+2+4+3 = 10.
19 is the largest bin edge, not a count. Sum the bar heights: 10.

steps.body: Binning trades detail for clarity: the 10-14 bar says four scores landed between 10 and 14, but NOT which exact scores. Unlike a dot plot, a histogram can't be read back into the original data. Same-width bins are non-negotiable — uneven bins make bar heights lie.

widget.prompt: Sort each score into its bin.

items.feedback: 3 falls between 0 and 4 — the first bin.
7 falls between 5 and 9 — the middle bin.
12 falls between 10 and 14 — the third bin.
9 is the TOP EDGE of the 5-9 bin — it still belongs there, not in 10-14.

widget.missFeedback: Compare each score to the bin edges: 0-4, 5-9, 10-14. Edge values belong to the bin that lists them.
widget.successFeedback: Binned — including the edge case: 9 belongs to 5-9.

explanationVariants: The bar records only that four scores landed in 10-14 — the exact values are not recoverable.
Histograms trade exact values for grouped clarity; dot plots keep every value.

widget.prompt: The 10-14 bar has height 4. Can you tell the four exact scores from the histogram?

options.label: No; the bar hides the exact scores
options.feedback: Right — binning groups values, losing the exact numbers. That's the price of the cleaner picture.

options.label: Yes; they are 10, 11, 12, and 13
options.feedback: They could be 11,12,12,14 or many other combinations — the bar doesn't say. Exact values are lost in binning.

options.label: Yes; the height gives the four scores
options.feedback: Height gives the COUNT (4), not the values themselves. The exact scores can't be recovered.

hints: Only the count inside the bin.

explanationVariants: With 200 varied values, individual dots would smear into noise — bins summarize; a small data set with few distinct values fits a dot plot perfectly.
Rule of thumb: few distinct values → dot plot; many spread-out values → histogram.

widget.prompt: You have 200 race times spread from 12 to 47 minutes. Which display fits better, and why?

options.label: A histogram with equal-width bins
options.feedback: Right — 200 dots over 35+ possible values would be unreadable; bins reveal the shape.

options.label: A dot plot with one dot per time
options.feedback: For 200 values across a wide range, the stacks become cluttered noise. Bins summarize better at this scale.

options.label: A list with all 200 race times
options.feedback: A raw list of 200 numbers hides the pattern that a picture reveals instantly. A histogram shows the shape at a glance.

hints: How many distinct values would dots need to cover?
Bins group the spread into a readable shape.
0-4 and 5-9 span five values each; 10-19 spans ten.
Uneven widths make bar heights incomparable.
explanationVariants: The bins 0-4, 5-9, 10-19 have unequal widths (5, 5, 10) — the wide bin collects more values just by being wider, so its height exaggerates.
Equal-width bins are what make heights comparable; a double-wide bin breaks the comparison.

widget.prompt: A student's histogram uses bins 0-4, 5-9, and 10-19. What's wrong with it?

options.label: The bins do not have equal widths
options.feedback: Right — a double-wide bin catches more values just by being wider, making its bar height misleading.

options.label: The bins may use any widths
options.feedback: Check the widths: 0-4 and 5-9 each cover 5 values, but 10-19 covers 10. Unequal bins make heights incomparable.

options.label: The display needs more bins
options.feedback: Three bins can be fine — the real problem is that they're not the SAME WIDTH: 5, 5, then 10.

takeaways: A histogram groups data into equal-width bins; bar height = count in that bin.
Bar heights sum to the data size, but exact values are lost to the grouping.
Few distinct values → dot plot; many spread-out values → histogram.
steps.teaser: chapter finale: describing a distribution's SHAPE.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Bar height counts the values inside the bin.** Bins 0-4 and 5-9 with data 2,3,7: the first bar is 2 tall (2 and 3), the second is 1 tall (just 7).

explanationVariants: The values 2 and 3 both land in 0-4, so that bar is 2 tall.
Count the data values inside the bin's range: two of them.

widget.prompt: Data: 2, 3, 7. Bins: 0-4 and 5-9. How tall is the 0-4 bar?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the bin's top EDGE, not its count. The values 2 and 3 land inside: height 2.
5 adds the values (2+3). Bar height COUNTS them instead: 2 values.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two values (2 and 3) land in 0-4: height 2.
